text:
A young man once approached a wise elder and confessed, “I said some terrible things about my friend. I was angry, and now I regret it. Can I take them back?”

The elder said nothing. He picked up a pillow, cut it open and walked with the young man to the top of a hill. “Shake out the feathers,” he said.

The young man did as he was told. The wind caught the feathers, and they scattered in every direction, across the fields, over the roofs and into the distance.

“Now,” said the elder, “go and collect them all.”

“That’s impossible!” cried the young man. “They’ve gone everywhere!”

“Yes,” said the elder. “Words are the same. Once spoken, they spread beyond our reach. We may apologise, and we should, but we can never gather them all back.”

The young man stared at the empty pillow. His eyes were wet. “What should I do?”

“First, go and apologise sincerely. Then, in the future, remember the feathers before you speak. Words are easy to release but impossible to retrieve.”

The young man went to his friend, humbly asked for forgiveness and received it. From that day, he paused before every difficult sentence and asked himself whether he was ready to watch it fly.

Moral: Speak carefully, because spoken words can never be fully taken back.

The young man collected all the feathers.
What did the elder cut open?
